points.name: りょ / おけ / おつ — texting abbreviations
points.shortDescription: Chat Japanese shortens everything, sometimes to a single character.
points.formation: Full phrase → first 1–3 moras (了解[りょうかい] → りょ)
points.explanation:
Japanese texting compresses hard. Many of these are too short to use out loud, and a few would be rude spoken — but in a chat window they are completely normal between friends.

Everyday chat clips:
- 了解[りょうかい] → りょ (or even り) — 'got it'
- オッケー → おけ — 'ok'
- お疲[つか]れさま → おつ — 'nice work / later'
- ありがとう → あざす / あざーす — 'thanks'
- とりあえずまあ → とりま — 'for now'
- おはよう → おは / おはよ

Seasonal set phrases, heard every January:
- あけましておめでとう → あけおめ
- 今年[ことし]もよろしく → ことよろ

The register rule is simple and strict: these belong to friends and casual group chats. Sending りょ to your boss reads roughly like replying 'k' to your manager in English. In a work chat, write 了解[りょうかい]しました or 承知[しょうち]しました.

Note also that り and りょ have a slightly juvenile, very-online feel even among young people — おけ and おつ are far safer.
rules: 了解[りょうかい] → りょ; オッケー → おけ; お疲[つか]れさま → おつ
ありがとう → あざす; とりあえずまあ → とりま
New Year: あけましておめでとう → あけおめ, 今年[ことし]もよろしく → ことよろ
Friends and casual group chats only — never to a boss or client
Work chat equivalents: 了解[りょうかい]しました / 承知[しょうち]しました

examples.japanese: 「五時[ごじ]集合[しゅうごう]ね」「りょ」

examples.english: Happy New Year! Looking forward to another year!
For now, let's just meet up.

points.flashcardHeader: りょ / おけ / おつ
points.flashcardAnswer: Chat clippings of 了解[りょうかい]・オッケー・お疲[つか]れさま. Friends-only; use 了解[りょうかい]しました at work.

practice.prompt: What is りょ short for?
practice.explanation: りょ (sometimes just り) clips 了解[りょうかい] — 'got it'. It is chat-only and quite casual.

practice.prompt: Your manager messages you a task on a work chat. What should you reply?
choices: 承知[しょうち]しました
practice.explanation: 承知[しょうち]しました is the professional acknowledgement. りょ or おけ would read like replying 'k' to your boss.

practice.prompt: What does あけおめ mean?
practice.explanation: あけおめ clips あけましておめでとう. It is usually paired with ことよろ (今年[ことし]もよろしく).

practice.prompt: What does おつ come from?
practice.explanation: おつ is clipped お疲[つか]れさま — used to sign off or acknowledge someone's effort among friends.

practice.prompt: What does とりま mean?
practice.explanation: とりま squeezes とりあえずまあ — 'for now, anyway'. Very casual and very common in chats.

points.name: Tone in text — 。、、、and small kana
points.shortDescription: Punctuation and kana size carry emotion that words alone don't.
points.formation: Small kana (〜ぁ, 〜ぉ) soften  |  、、、 trails off  |  ！ warms  |  。 can chill
points.explanation:
Japanese chat is written, so all the tone that voice normally carries has to live in the typing itself. A few conventions do most of the work.

Ending punctuation:
- No punctuation at all is the friendly default: わかった
- ！ warms things up: わかった！
- A full stop can read as cold or curt: わかった。 In some group chats this is the equivalent of a flat 'fine.'
- 、、、 or … trails off, showing hesitation or discomfort: 明日[あした]はちょっと、、、

Small kana soften and cutesify the end of a word: そっかぁ, ですぅ, ねぇ. Stretching with ー does similar work: そうだよねー.

Katakana can be used for emphasis or a dry, ironic tone even on native words: ダメ, ヤバい, スゴイ.

And repeated w or 草[くさ] scales laughter: w is a chuckle, www is real laughter, wwwww is helpless.

None of this is in a textbook, but misreading it causes real friction — a learner who ends every message with 。 can come across as annoyed without ever knowing it.
rules: No punctuation = friendly default; ！ adds warmth
A bare 。 can read cold or curt in casual chat
、、、 / … signals hesitation, discomfort, or a soft refusal
Small kana (そっかぁ, ねぇ) and stretched ー soften the tone
Katakana on native words adds emphasis or dry irony: ダメ, スゴイ

examples.japanese: 明日[あした]はちょっと、、、
そっかぁ、残念[ざんねん]だねー。

points.flashcardAnswer: Punctuation and kana size carry emotion: ！ warms, bare 。 chills, 、、、 hesitates, small kana softens.

practice.prompt: In a casual chat, how can ending with a plain 。 come across?
practice.explanation: Casual chat usually drops end punctuation, so adding 。 can read as flat or annoyed — like replying 'Fine.' in English.

practice.prompt: What does 、、、 at the end of a message signal?
practice.japanese: 明日[あした]はちょっと、、、
practice.explanation: Trailing dots leave the sentence unfinished, which in Japanese usually signals reluctance — here, a polite no.

practice.prompt: What does the small ぁ in そっかぁ do?
practice.explanation: Small kana stretch and soften the ending, giving a gentler, more emotional feel than そっか alone.

practice.prompt: What does writing a native word in katakana (ダメ, スゴイ) often add?
choices: Emphasis or a dry, ironic tone
practice.explanation: Katakana on a native word works like italics — emphasis, or a slightly detached, ironic delivery.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between w and wwwww?
choices: Length scales the amount of laughter
practice.explanation: w is a small chuckle; repeating it scales up the laughter, with wwwww reading as helpless laughing.

points.name: ググる / バズる / サボる — turning nouns into verbs
points.shortDescription: Japanese verbs almost any noun by bolting る onto the end.
points.formation: Noun (often clipped to 2 moras) + る, conjugated as a Group 1 verb
points.explanation:
One of the most productive habits in modern Japanese: take a noun — usually foreign, usually clipped to two syllables — and add る to make a verb. It then conjugates exactly like a normal Group 1 verb.

- Google → ググる (to google): ググった, ググって
- buzz → バズる (to go viral): バズってる
- disrespect → ディスる (to diss)
- sabotage → サボる (to skip class / slack off) — this one is decades old and fully standard
- Twitter → ツイート/つぶやく; memo → メモる (to jot down)
- panic → パニクる; negotiate/miss → ミスる (to screw up)

Because they behave like ordinary verbs, all the normal forms work: ググれば, ググりたい, ググらないで.

Age matters here. サボる and メモる are completely neutral and used by everyone. ググる is universal too. バズる and ディスる are newer and read as young or media-flavoured. New ones appear constantly, so the pattern is more useful to learn than any individual word.
rules: Noun + る creates a Group 1 verb: ググる, バズる, サボる, メモる
Conjugates normally: ググった, ググって, ググれば
サボる (skip/slack) and メモる (jot down) are fully standard, not slang
バズる and ディスる are newer and sound young or media-ish
The pattern is productive — new coinages appear all the time

examples.japanese: わからないならググって。
examples.english: If you don't know, just google it.

examples.japanese: あの動画[どうが]、バズってるらしいよ。
examples.english: That video is apparently going viral.

examples.japanese: 授業[じゅぎょう]をサボった。
忘[わす]れる前[まえ]にメモっとく。
examples.english: I'll jot it down before I forget.

points.flashcardHeader: ググる / バズる / サボる
points.flashcardAnswer: Noun + る makes a Group 1 verb. サボる and メモる are standard; バズる and ディスる sound newer.

practice.prompt: What does ググって mean?
practice.explanation: ググる is 'to google', formed from Google + る. ググって is its て-form used as a casual request.

practice.prompt: Which of these is fully standard, not slang?
practice.explanation: サボる (from 'sabotage') has been in everyday Japanese for decades and is used by all ages without any slang feel.

practice.prompt: What does バズってる mean?
practice.explanation: バズる comes from English 'buzz' — to blow up online. バズってる is the progressive: 'it's going viral right now'.

practice.prompt: Put ググる into the past tense.
practice.explanation: These behave like normal Group 1 verbs ending in る, so the past is ググった.

practice.prompt: What is the general pattern behind these verbs?
practice.explanation: A noun, usually shortened to about two moras, takes る and then conjugates like any Group 1 verb.

points.name: 既読[きどく] / スタンプ — LINE and messaging culture
points.shortDescription: The vocabulary and unwritten rules of Japan's dominant messaging app.
points.formation: 既読[きどく] (read) ・未読[みどく] (unread) ・既読[きどく]スルー ・スタンプ ・グループ
points.explanation:
LINE is the default messaging app in Japan, and it comes with its own vocabulary and social pressures that learners run into quickly.

Core words:
- 既読[きどく] — 'read'. LINE shows the sender when you have opened their message.
- 未読[みどく] — unread.
- 既読[きどく]スルー (kidoku suru) — reading a message and not replying. A genuine social sore point, sometimes shortened to KS.
- 未読[みどく]スルー — not even opening it.
- スタンプ — sticker. Used constantly, often *instead* of words.
- 通話[つうわ] — a voice call; グループ — a group chat.
- 送[おく]る / 返[かえ]す — to send / to reply back.

The unwritten rules matter as much as the words. A sticker alone is a perfectly complete reply — sending one is not lazy, it is normal, and it neatly ends a conversation without the awkwardness of a bare 'ok'. Reply speed carries meaning too, and leaving a friend on 既読[きどく] for a long time can read as a snub even when nothing was meant by it.

Group chats often run on stickers and one-word replies, so being able to read them matters more than being able to compose long messages.
rules: 既読[きどく] = read, 未読[みどく] = unread
既読[きどく]スルー = reading a message and not replying — socially loaded
スタンプ (stickers) can be a complete reply on their own
通話[つうわ] = voice call; グループ = group chat
Reply speed carries meaning — long silences after 既読[きどく] can read as a snub

examples.japanese: 既読[きどく]ついてるのに返事[へんじ]がない。
examples.romaji: Kidoku tsuiteru noni henji ga nai.
examples.english: It's marked as read but there's no reply.

examples.japanese: ごめん、既読[きどく]スルーしちゃった。
examples.english: Sorry, I read it and forgot to reply.

examples.japanese: スタンプだけ送[おく]っといた。
あとで通話[つうわ]しよう。
examples.english: Let's do a voice call later.

points.flashcardHeader: 既読[きどく] / スタンプ
points.flashcardAnswer: LINE vocabulary: 既読[きどく] (read), 既読[きどく]スルー (read and ignored), スタンプ (stickers, a complete reply).

practice.prompt: What does 既読[きどく] mean on LINE?
practice.explanation: 既読[きどく] appears once you open a message, letting the sender know it has been read. 未読[みどく] is the opposite.

practice.prompt: What is 既読[きどく]スルー?
choices: Reading a message and not replying
practice.explanation: 既読[きどく] (read) + スルー (from English 'through', meaning to ignore). It is a common source of friction between friends.

practice.prompt: Is replying with only a スタンプ considered rude?
choices: No — it is a normal, complete reply
practice.explanation: Stickers are a standard way to reply and to close a conversation politely without a blunt one-word message.

practice.prompt: What does 未読[みどく] mean?
practice.explanation: 未[み] means 'not yet', so 未読[みどく] is 'not yet read' — the opposite of 既読[きどく].

practice.prompt: Why does reply speed matter on LINE?
choices: The 既読[きどく] marker makes silence visible
practice.explanation: Because the sender can see exactly when you read it, a long gap after 既読[きどく] is visible and can be read as a snub.

vocab.definition: got it (chat form of 了解)
reading a message and not replying
